name: Opus 5 dispersion
strategy: Beta-matched dispersion rebuilt for a Fed-hiking, 5.24% 10-year regime: a 55% long basket of eleven large caps across eleven sectors, screened for residual-to-SPY volatility and low pairwise residual correlation, with leverage-sensitive and secular-decline names removed and two rate-up beneficiaries (CME, TRV) added as the offsetting counterweight to the inflation-hedge legs (NEM, SLB), hedged with a 38% SPY short sized to the basket's 0.68 estimated beta for net index beta of roughly zero, 7% cash.
reassessment_note: The last leg lost ~1.6% with ten of thirteen longs red while SPY rallied 1.79%. That is not dispersion noise, it is a systematic factor loss, and diagnosing it is the reason I am trading rather than holding. The screen's 'deliberately offsetting macro loadings' were estimated on a pre-shock window and did not offset: the Fed actually HIKED on 2026-09-16 (my entry day), the 10-year is at 5.24% (highest since 2007) with 65% odds of another hike in October, and every levered or duration-sensitive long fell together. The basket had an unintended common factor - leverage and long-duration value - that the SPY hedge does not neutralize, because shorting the index hedges beta, not a factor tilt. Four cuts, all thesis breaks rather than drawdowns I am flinching at. CHTR is the clearest: ~$93B of debt in a hiking cycle on top of a genuine secular broadband decline (Comcast's sector warning, Wolfe cut to Underperform with a $118 target the stock has already broken), eight straight down days, and at $111.40 it sits 3% above its stop - holding it is just waiting to be stopped out, and it was the single largest contributor to the loss. CF goes because its drawdown came from an unforecastable political headline (Trump-Belarus potash) plus cooling nitrogen prices; a dispersion book wants idiosyncratic risk, not policy risk. GPN goes because at $84.70 against an $84.29 consensus target it offers residual volatility with no edge, and 'payments as a rate-up beneficiary' was always the weakest link in the original screen. MRNA is a harvest, not a loss: +35.5% on this leg and +550% YTD on a single melanoma-vaccine catalyst. Because a re-registered leg resets the entry basis, keeping it is not protecting a gain - it is a fresh decision to buy a parabolic name at $197, which is a momentum bet and not what this book does. I take the win. The adds lean into the regime I can actually identify rather than the one I wish for. TRV is the cleanest rate-up beneficiary available: 25% of a $92.9B fixed-maturity portfolio rolls into materially higher reinvestment yields, NII already +14%, EPS estimated +22.6%. CI is a re-rating candidate at $271.83 against a $357 consensus with earnings on Oct 29, safely outside this horizon. I sized CME up to top weight because rate volatility is its raw material - record ADV of 27M contracts and a 69.5% operating margin - and its 3.4% pullback improves the entry. I kept NEM and SLB deliberately: with gold at $4,350 and oil near $98 they are the inflation-up legs that offset CME and TRV, which benefit from hikes that fight inflation, and that is the offsetting structure working as designed rather than the version that failed. LVS stays and earns its keep as the one leg orthogonal to the entire US rate story, with Macau Golden Week starting Oct 1 as a near-term catalyst and the stock at a 58% discount to its five-year average EV/EBITDA. The SPY hedge drops from 40.3% to 38% purely as arithmetic: removing the high-beta levered names and adding TRV, CI and DG lowers the basket's weighted beta to ~0.68, so a smaller short keeps net beta at roughly zero. I have deliberately left the SPY short with NO stop-loss. The desk notes four short-leg stops fired last week on a 1.55% SPY rally; a stop on an index hedge is actively harmful, because it strips the hedge precisely when a rally means the basket most needs it, converting a market-neutral book into an unhedged long at the worst moment. Stops on the longs stay wide enough not to be shaken out by residual noise, which is the volatility this book is paid to hold, and are tightened only on HII where the cash-flow risk is real.

positions.thesis: Top weight and the single cleanest expression of the regime: rate volatility is CME's raw material, not its risk. With the 10-year at 5.24%, the Fed hiking and 65%/53% odds of further hikes in October/December, hedging demand is structural - record ADV of 27M contracts (+23%), all-time open-interest highs in Ultra 10-Year and Ultra Bond futures, credit futures volume +164% YTD, on a 69.5% adjusted operating margin. Sized up from 5.1% because the thesis strengthened while the stock fell 3.4%, improving the entry. Its macro loading is the deliberate counterweight to the inflation-hedge legs NEM and SLB.

New. The most direct rate-up beneficiary I can own without taking credit risk: a $92.9B fixed-maturity portfolio with five-year duration, of which ~25% matures within three years and reinvests at the highest yields since 2007. Net investment income is already +14% to $1.07B with management guiding $840M/$870M after-tax fixed-income NII for Q3/Q4, and consensus EPS growth of +22.6%. Unlike the value names I cut, it is working - up 26.9% YTD against SPX +12.4% - so it is not a falling knife, and at ~0.65 beta it lowers the basket's hedge requirement. Verified NYSE-listed at $363.16 on the 2026-09-28 close.

New. Managed care is one of the few large-cap pockets whose residual volatility comes from medical-cost trend and reimbursement policy - drivers with near-zero loading on rates, oil, gold or AI capex, which is exactly the orthogonality this book is screening for. Cigna raised guidance and grew profit in Q2 across both health services and pharmacy benefits, yet trades at $271.83 against a $357.76 consensus target. Earnings on Oct 29 sit outside this horizon, so I am holding the re-rating, not a binary event. Held at 5.5% rather than larger because it shares some drug-pricing policy exposure with MCK, and I am capping that common factor. Verified NYSE-listed at $271.83 on the 2026-09-28 close.

One of only three longs that worked last leg (+3.01% against a basket that was broadly red), which is evidence its residual is genuinely independent of the leverage factor that sank CHTR and CF. Ag machinery runs on farm income and replacement cycles rather than the rate path, and it carries the basket's highest beta (~0.95), which is priced into the hedge rather than left unmanaged. Trimmed from 5.1% only to make room for the rate-up adds.

Drug distribution is fee-for-service on prescription volume, making revenue close to macro-inert - no oil, gold, rate or China loading - which is precisely why it belongs in a dispersion basket. The -3.49% drawdown was sector drift, not a thesis break, and nothing in the research contradicts the original case. Trimmed slightly from 5.1% to cap combined healthcare-channel exposure alongside the new CI position, since both carry shared drug-pricing policy risk.

The second of three longs that worked last leg (+1.11%). Its macro loading is the deliberate inverse of LVS: persistently elevated inflation and a Fed hiking into a squeezed consumer pushes trade-down traffic into discount retail at the same time it pressures discretionary gaming spend, so the pair is self-offsetting inside the basket. At ~0.35 beta it is the lowest-beta long, materially reducing the SPY short the book must carry.

Best performer among the survivors (+4.32%) and the book's only technology exposure, deliberately chosen because edge delivery and security are subscription-driven and carry no AI-capex loading - critical when AI leadership is the dominant factor this book refuses to hedge into. Wider 18% stop because its residual volatility is the highest-quality dispersion in the basket and I do not want to be shaken out of the noise I am paid to hold.

Retained but cut from 5.1% and the stop tightened from 18% to 16%, because the -7.57% drawdown reflects a real issue rather than noise: negative free cash flow in H1 from heavy investment against Navy contracts, with Bernstein cutting its target to $337 and flagging that throughput and margin conversion are not yet there. The offset is that multi-decade submarine backlog is the most rate-insensitive revenue stream available, management guides positive FCF for Q3, Q4 and full-year 2026, and at $257 the stock is far below a $368 consensus. Smaller size is how I hold a genuinely uncorrelated asset whose near-term execution I do not fully trust.

Sized up from 3.7% and kept deliberately as the inflation-up counterweight to CME and TRV, which profit from hikes that succeed in suppressing inflation - if the Fed wins, the rate legs carry the book; if inflation stays sticky at 5.24% yields, gold does. Gold's pullback to $4,350 on hawkish signals is the entry, not the thesis break: at that price and $1,680 AISC on ~5.3Moz of attributable production the margin is extraordinary, and the stock at $116 sits below Bernstein's $157 and BofA's $151. Take-profit at 35% because gold equities spike rather than grind.

The single leg whose driver sits entirely outside the US rate story - Macau gross gaming revenue and the Chinese consumer - which is the highest-value orthogonality in the book when a common US-macro factor is what damaged the last leg. Macau Golden Week begins Oct 1, immediately after entry, giving a near-term idiosyncratic catalyst into peak seasonality; the stock has been upgraded on Macau share gains, trades at a 58% discount to its five-year average forward EV/EBITDA and at $39 against a ~$59 consensus. Oct 21 earnings sit beyond this week's horizon. Held at 4% because the China consumer risk is genuine and unhedgeable.

The oil-up leg, retained at reduced weight as the second half of the inflation-hedge pairing with NEM. Crude near $98 remains historically elevated and keeps international and offshore service pricing firm, and the -1.55% drawdown is immaterial noise rather than a thesis break. Kept as the smallest long because oilfield services is levered to E&P capex rather than the spot commodity itself, which makes it the less direct inflation expression of the two, and because SLB carries ~1.05 beta that the hedge must fund.

The beta hedge that makes this a dispersion book rather than a long basket. Sized by arithmetic, not by view: the rebuilt basket's weighted beta is ~0.68 on 55% gross long, contributing ~37.6 percentage points of SPY-equivalent exposure, so a 38% short leaves net index beta at roughly zero. It is smaller than last leg's 40.3% purely because removing the levered high-beta names (CHTR, CF) and adding TRV, CI and DG lowered the basket's beta. Deliberately carries NO stop-loss: the desk notes four short-leg stops fired last week on a 1.55% SPY rally, and a stop on an index hedge is self-defeating, because it removes the hedge exactly when a rally means the long basket most needs it and silently converts a market-neutral book into an unhedged long at the worst possible moment. Short borrow at 3% APR is the known cost of carrying it.
